The sleep framework: A new way for LLMs to retain knowledge in continual learning
summary: Google Research introduces a sleep framework for continual LLM learning that alternates between active interaction and offline memory consolidation phases. The framework addresses catastrophic forgetting by using Mixture-of-Experts memory blocks and self-generated practice examples during sleep phases, enabling models to retain knowledge up to 10M tokens and improve reasoning without static knowledge cutoffs. Key results include near-perfect scaling on long-context tasks, 46.2% accuracy on factual knowledge incorporation, and 79.2% on AIME mathematical reasoning—outperforming baselines like GPT-4 and standard fine-tuning. For deployed systems, this enables continuous adaptation while preserving existing capabilities through structured memory consolidation and gradient-based sample selection during autonomous self-improvement cycles.

title: How Anthropic ships Claude with Claude: Separating the Brain from the Hands
summary: Anthropic ships Claude Opus 5.5 with major cost reductions and improved clarity while implementing anti-distillation measures like preserved thinking blocks across turns. The company separates agent "brains" (session harness) from "hands" (execution sandbox) for better security and reliability—a key architectural pattern for safe agent deployment. For builders, the critical takeaway: isolate untrusted code execution from credentials and session state, use trust grants for fine-grained access control, and invest heavily in safety infrastructure as model capabilities increase, not just feature velocity.

Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3
summary: Liquid AI released LFM3, a family of 2B-parameter multimodal foundation models designed for on-device deployment and specialization. The tri-hybrid architecture (gated convolutions, sliding-window attention, global attention) achieves 35% better efficiency than LFM2, with LFM3-1.7B outperforming LFM2.5-2.6B. Six specialized variants cover text, vision, audio, omni, and decision tasks, each fine-tunable on a single GPU with custom encoders reducing compute requirements. For builders, this enables deploying domain-specific models locally with minimal resources—LFM3-1.7B fits in 1GB at 4-bit precision with 256K context, while LFM3-Omni-2B beats Qwen2.5-Omni-7B on audio-visual understanding despite being 3.5x smaller.

title: Can we trust LLMs to judge whether a research idea is novel?
summary: Allen AI released NoveltyBench, a benchmark evaluating how reliably LLMs judge research novelty, using ICLR peer reviews to identify high and low novelty ideas. Testing six models (GPT-5.1-5.4, Claude Sonnet/Opus variants), they found prompt changes alone shift accuracy by 50+ percentage points, with instability especially severe on AI-generated ideas. Surprisingly, simple Claude Opus 4.6 prompting outperformed expensive purpose-built systems like AI Scientist ($82) and Idea Novelty Checker ($31), achieving 0.854 macro-F1 at $2.59. The key takeaway: novelty evaluation is brittle and unreliable for AI-generated ideas—a critical gap for automated scientific discovery systems.

3 Ways to Boost MoE Inference on NVIDIA DGX Spark
summary: NVIDIA published three techniques for accelerating MoE inference on DGX Spark using Ling-3.0-flash (124B parameters, 5.1B active). The optimizations—Humming MXFP4 MoE kernels, online FP8 LM-head quantization, and multi-token prediction speculative decoding—address memory-bound bottlenecks in batch-size-1 decoding. Combined, they achieve 42.5% throughput improvement and 24.5% latency reduction on GSM8K with no accuracy loss. Critical takeaway: when stacking all three, the draft model must share the full LM-head module; otherwise the system silently degrades below baseline performance.
